claim: Joe Biden wants to ban fracking
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (CNN, AP, NBC, Washington Post, Newsweek) from the exact time period found that Biden's actual written policy only proposed banning new oil and gas permits on federal public lands, not a nationwide fracking ban, and that Biden repeatedly and explicitly denied wanting to ban fracking. While Biden's past primary-debate comments created genuine confusion that partially justified the attack, fact-checkers consistently rated the blanket claim that 'Biden wants to ban fracking' as false or misleading.

trace.raw_text:
Based on multiple independent fact-checks from CNN, NBC News, AP, Washington Post, and Newsweek, this claim was consistently rated as false or misleading during the 2020 campaign.

Biden's actual written policy called for banning new oil and gas permits (including new fracking) only on federal public lands, not a nationwide fracking ban. Biden is not running on a proposal to completely ban fracking and it was never part of his written plan. Biden has explicitly said he does not support a nationwide fracking ban. AP's fact-check was direct: "THE FACTS: That's false. Biden has repeatedly pledged not to abolish fracking."

That said, fact-checkers noted the issue was genuinely muddled by some of Biden's own past remarks. It's false that Biden never said he opposed fracking. In two Democratic primary debates, Biden made confusing remarks over fracking that his campaign had to clarify. In 2019, Biden said "we would make sure it's eliminated" when asked about the future of coal and fracking; in 2020 he said he opposed "new fracking." However, the Biden campaign clarified to reporters that Biden was reiterating his plan to ban oil and gas permits on public land, not a complete ban on new fracking, which a president cannot do. Biden's written plan proposes "banning new oil and gas permitting on public lands and waters," not ending all new fracking anywhere.

Multiple outlets concluded the Trump campaign's specific claim — that Biden "wants to ban fracking" nationally — was an inaccurate characterization of his actual policy, even while acknowledging Biden's rhetoric had at times been inconsistent. it's also inaccurate for Trump to claim Biden's current plan is to end fracking if elected.

claim: The U.S. surgeon general and the Centers for Disease Control both previously said that ‘masks are not effective in preventing [the] general public from catching coronavirus.’
justification: Multiple independent news sources (Bloomberg, CNN, The Hill, Time, CBS News, Wikipedia) confirm that Surgeon General Jerome Adams tweeted on Feb 29, 2020 that masks 'are NOT effective in preventing general public from catching Coronavirus,' explicitly citing CDC guidance, and that the CDC itself did not recommend masks for healthy members of the public at that time. This was official U.S. government messaging from Feb-March 2020, before it was reversed on April 3, 2020.

The evidence strongly confirms this claim. On February 29, 2020, Surgeon General Jerome Adams tweeted "Seriously people- STOP BUYING MASKS! They are NOT effective in preventing general public from catching #Coronavirus, but if healthcare providers can't get them to care for sick patients, it puts them and our communities at risk!" His post also linked to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines, noting that the CDC does not recommend that healthy people wear medical masks to protect themselves from respiratory diseases, including coronavirus.

This messaging was consistent across the government at the time — the U.S. government did not recommend the use of face masks by the general public outside of medical settings to protect themselves from COVID-19, as to prevent shortages of medical-grade personal protective equipment (PPE) for doctors treating COVID-19 patients. Adams reiterated this stance on national television, telling CBS News in March 2020 that "Masks do not work for the general public and preventing them from getting coronavirus."

The CDC's position was the same at the time: "What the World Health Organization and the CDC have reaffirmed in the last few days is that they do not recommend the general public wear masks." This guidance later reversed — on April 3, 2020, the CDC issued guidance recommending that non-medical face coverings be worn in public when social distancing is difficult to maintain — but the claim specifically refers to what was "previously" said, which matches the February–March 2020 timeframe.

Adams later acknowledged the reversal, telling CBS's Face the Nation in July 2020: "When we learn better, we do better." He explained that the CDC, World Health Organization and a New England Journal of Medicine article in May all indicated that masks were not effective at the time he made his original statement.

claim: Germany’s Foreign Minister Heiko Maas said that Thailand’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn didn’t do anything illegal while at his German residence.
justification: On 26-27 October 2020, Maas's actual public remarks were cautionary — he said Germany was monitoring the King's activities and that illegal conduct 'would have immediate consequences,' not that the King had done nothing illegal. The clear statement that the King 'had not done anything illegal' was issued by the German Government in November 2020, weeks after the claimed date, and was not a direct personal statement from Maas but a government response to a protester letter.

trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, the claim contains a mix of accurate and inaccurate elements regarding both the substance and timing of the statement.

**What the sources actually show:**

On the specific date cited (27 October 2020), Maas's public statements were notably more cautious than the claim suggests. At a press conference around 26 October 2020, Maas said "We have not only been looking into that in recent weeks, but on a regular basis," and "If there are things we consider to be illegal, that will have immediate consequences." This is a statement about ongoing monitoring and a conditional warning — not a declaration that the King "didn't do anything illegal."

Similarly, a more detailed account of that period shows Maas saying: at a press conference with the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency in Berlin on 26 October 2020, Federal Foreign Minister Maas was asked about the Thai King in Germany. The Minister replied that he was "keeping an eye on what the Thai King is up to in Germany," and that "if there are things that we perceive to be illegal, then this will have immediate consequences."

A day later, on 28 October, a parliamentary briefing gave a more nuanced picture: In a briefing to the Foreign Affairs Committee of the Federal Parliament, the Government seemed to paint a more nuanced picture; a parliamentary source said the Federal Government believed the King was permitted to make occasional decisions, as long as he did not continuously conduct business, and that the Government was not yet of the opinion that he had continuously conducted business from German soil. Al Jazeera similarly reported that Germany does not believe that Thailand's king has so far breached its ban on conducting politics during his extended periods in the country, according to a parliamentary source — this was attributed to a "parliamentary source," not directly to Maas.

The clear statement that the King "had not done anything illegal" actually came **later, in November 2020**, and was attributed to the German Government generally rather than to Maas personally: In November, the German Government issued a statement confirming that King Vajiralongkorn had not done anything illegal while living in the country, in response to a letter from protesters delivered to the German embassy in Bangkok.

**Assessment:** The substance of the claim (that German authorities eventually said the King had not acted illegally) is broadly accurate, but it happened in November 2020 via a general government statement — not on 27 October 2020, and not as a direct quote from Maas himself. On the date specified, Maas's actual remarks were more guarded, emphasizing monitoring and warning of "consequences" if illegal conduct were found, rather than a clearance of wrongdoing.

In late March/early April 2020, following a phone call between Presidents Trump and Putin, Russia sent a military plane carrying protective gear and ventilators to the United States on Wednesday to help the country battle the deadly coronavirus outbreak. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed this, stating "Trump gratefully accepted this humanitarian aid," and the shipment reportedly included 60 tons of ventilators, masks, respirators and other items.

claim: India's imports from China increased by 27% during the period April-August 2020.
justification: Multiple sources, including a PIB Fact Check response and government data from Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal's statement to Parliament, confirm that India's imports from China actually DECREASED by 27.63% during April-August 2020, while it was India's EXPORTS to China that increased by 27% during that period. Pachauri appears to have conflated imports and exports, and later posted a partial correction acknowledging the error while still maintaining a broader point about trade dynamics.

trace.raw_text:
Based on the search results, this claim is clearly false and was officially debunked at the time.

@PankajPachauri claimed in a tweet that India's imports from China have increased by 27% during April-August. This claim was flagged as Fake by PIB Fact Check, which noted India's imports from China decreased by 27.63% whereas India's exports to China increased by 27% during the same period.

The actual figures come from the government itself: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal told Parliament that India's imports from China declined by 27.63 per cent during April-August that fiscal to USD 21.58 billion over the same period previous year.

Pachauri had conflated the two figures — imports actually fell by roughly that percentage, while it was exports that rose 27%. Pachauri later acknowledged this on Twitter, posting a "Corrigendum" stating that a government functionary pointed out it was exports, not imports, that increased 27% from April onward, though he maintained that trade with China was increasing while there was an "eyeball to eyeball situation at LAC," and that China's share in India's trade had also increased.

Independent trade data corroborates the fact-check: for the April-July period, India's total imports declined by 48 per cent in the April-July period compared to a year ago, but the decline in imports from China was much slower — the figure contracted by 29 per cent, while India's exports to China rose 31 per cent in the April-July period — confirming it was exports, not imports, that grew.

This claim has been directly fact-checked by Africa Check, an independent fact-checking organization, in an article published on 14 September 2020 (shortly after the claim circulated on social media following the death of Nathaniel Julies).

According to Africa Check's investigation: comparing SAPS annual reports, the department had a total of 132,310 employees in 2002/03, and the latest annual report showed 192,277 employees in 2018/19. Using total headcount figures, these figures indicate that the police force grew by 45.3% over the period.

However, those totals include non-police administrative staff. The figures include public service act employees who provide organisational and administrative support to the police. When they are excluded, police personnel numbers stood at 102,737 in 2002/03 and 150,885 in 2018/19. Using the UN's stricter definition of police personnel (those with law enforcement functions), the UN defines police personnel as "those whose principal functions are the prevention, detection and investigation of crime and the apprehension of alleged offenders", and using this measure, South Africa's police force has grown by 47% since 2002.

Africa Check's overall conclusion was that a claim that South Africa's police force has grown by 50% since 2002 is mostly correct. The actual growth (45.3%–47% depending on methodology) is close to but slightly below the stated 50% figure — a reasonably accurate rounding of the underlying data rather than a fabrication.

It's also worth noting that this growth trend has since reversed: the number of staff in SAPS has declined steadily over the past decade, from a peak total staff complement of 199,345 in 2011/12 to 182,126 at the end of the 2020/2021 financial year, but that later decline doesn't affect the accuracy of the original 2002–2020 growth claim being checked here.
